entries.title: Inside Nvidia, Not Everyone Is Celebrating Jensen Huang’s Return
entries.summary: Some saw Huang’s resignation as an opportunity for culture change at the chip giant. “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again,” one employee said.
entries.content:
Jensen Huang received a “hero’s welcome” from employees on Monday after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated him as CEO, according to people who were present. An outspoken faction of Nvidia’s workforce had demanded his return and greeted him with chants, raucous applause, and hugs at the company’s headquarters.

But other employees were quietly stewing. Several current and former Nvidia staffers had viewed Huang’s abrupt exit earlier this month as a rare opportunity to change the “one team” corporate culture of unfettered unity and minimal bureaucracy that he had cultivated over the past three decades, according to interviews with the workers, as well as internal correspondence and social media posts reviewed by WIRED. Most spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared backlash from colleagues.

Some employees were alarmed by Huang’s alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate and another with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. But their frustrations extended beyond the CEO’s personal conduct. Current and former workers describe a culture at Nvidia in which allegedly abusive behavior was tolerated and challenging leadership was perceived as discouraged.

“Everyone agrees that mistakes were made, the question is what we are ready to forgive,” one employee wrote on an internal platform before Huang’s return. “I don’t know how comfortable I’ll be working at a place where such affairs are not taken extremely seriously.”

Another added, “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

When Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices in California on Monday, he told employees who greeted him that he would do a better job with his second chance at CEO. (As of Monday afternoon, he had not yet sent a companywide note about his return, as he was still getting his laptop set back up.)

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at Peard33.24

US President Donald Trump said he played a crucial role in convincing Nvidia's board to bring back Huang. A person close to Trump calls him an irreplaceable CEO and says they expect him to exercise better judgement going forward.

Nvidia’s board announced it will continue an independent investigation into whether Huang had been a target of foreign intelligence services and that it will double down on plans to step up corporate governance.

It’s difficult to gauge how widespread dissatisfaction with Huang’s leadership may be at Nvidia. The company’s emphasis on unity has historically made it difficult for people to openly question his leadership or choices, workers say. “There's only one team at NVIDIA,” the chipmaker’s official website declares.

A public petition campaign known as Stand with Jensen garnered signatures from more than 10,000 Nvidia purported employees, according to its website. Nvidia has roughly 49,000 employees and 18,000 contractors overall, according to a person familiar with its workforce.

But inside Nvidia, one employee told colleagues that “some portion” of the signatures appeared to be “illegitimate,” noting that the names included “Satan” and media personality Mia Khalifa, who does not work at the chipmaker. The employee wrote that they found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking. WIRED was unable to independently verify the findings. The petition’s organizers did not respond to requests for comment.

Huang’s supporters have praised how he made the company feel like a “big super family.” They credited him for minimizing bureaucracy, making himself available to staff, and supporting employees during difficult periods, including the Covid pandemic. A former employee who attended numerous meetings with Huang and other senior executives says the CEO was particularly adept at preventing bureaucratic infighting. He could detect corporate “politics and nonsense before it was even born,” says the worker.

There are also powerful financial reasons for Nvidia employees to feel loyal to Huang. His bets on chips and software for artificial intelligence have transformed Nvidia into one of the world’s most valuable companies and made many longtime employees wealthy in the process.

But for some employees, the revelations about Huang’s behavior have forced them to question that loyalty. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader at Nvidia, wrote on LinkedIn last week that he ultimately couldn’t decide whether he wanted Huang back as he weighed arguments from both sides. “Some believe his contributions to NVIDIA and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” Sequeira wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. … I don’t have a clear answer.”

Several current and former workers say that Huang’s management style could come off as overly harsh at times, including, for example, toward longtime colleagues he viewed as having grown complacent as Nvidia’s market value surged. Two former employees say that he regularly raised his voice at workers, sometimes in ways they found belittling.

Other employees were more concerned about whether Nvidia’s board would hold Huang accountable for allegedly misleading the directors about his affairs. “That’s something we can’t have,” one employee says.

Another source of frustration for Nvidia workers has been the growing influence of Huang’s two children and son-in-law, who all hold senior titles at the chipmaker. In March, his daughter, Madison Huang scolded a colleague on a call with about 100 other employees, according to a participant who didn’t believe the anger was warranted. “I’m disappointed you asked that, are you fucking stupid?” the employee recalls Madison saying in response to a question about workshops on OpenClaw technology scheduled for an upcoming Nvidia conference. “Your mom can build a claw.”

Madison and her brother, Spencer Huang, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Praveen Mhapsekar, a senior system software engineer who was let go last week after disputes with his managers and HR, says he and colleagues stopped feeling comfortable complaining about practices that concerned them because of the trouble they believe it brought on themselves.

“This organization requires greater discipline and structured processes,” he says. One of the world’s most valuable companies “cannot be managed like a private startup operating out of a garage, where personal influence takes precedence over established procedures.”

Huang’s return doesn’t eliminate the prospect of Nvidia evolving to quell frustrations. But with internal issues more public than ever before, maybe the days of one big family all cheering along together are mostly gone.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode and Hugo Lowell.

entries.title: How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump
entries.summary: Prediction market traders profited from the Nvidia CEO’s comeback by following the White House’s lead. “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” says one winner.
entries.content:
Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior, Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped 6 percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, the odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to returning, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when Trump threw his support behind the former CEO.

But Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode also identified clusters of trades that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and long-shot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and a professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says that he figured the board would consider Huang’s return if it looked likely to improve the company’s stock performance. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “pee in your brain.”)

“It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

entries.title: The Feds Left Iowans in the Dark About Plans to Blow Up Tons of Lead
entries.summary: The US Army plans to blow up 9,500 pounds of lead azide held at an Iowa ammunition plant. Local officials say they learned most of the details through a press release.
entries.content:
On October 26, Charles Massner, the mayor of Mediapolis, Iowa, got an email from the US Army. It described “an intentional, controlled detonation” of “a quantity of degraded lead azide … in the near future” at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, some 20 miles south of Mediapolis.

The email, which was reviewed by WIRED, provided no details about when this explosion would happen, how much material the explosion would destroy, or what steps officials should take to protect the public from a possible toxic fallout. But it did request that public officials allow for environmental testing on public lands before and after the event, which the town granted in a November 2 meeting.

Massner says the next time he heard anything was early last week, when the Army published a press release on its website saying it would explode the lead azide in just a few days. That press release included a map of potential exposure from the blast. Mediapolis was directly in the path of exposure, covered in a reddish-yellow cloud with a hot pink border.

“There was really no communication, so to speak, other than what was on their website,” he says.

Massner wasn’t alone in being caught off guard. The sudden announcement that the Army would be exploding 9,500 pounds of lead azide with seemingly little to no notice caught nearly all of Iowa by surprise. Governor Kim Reynolds’ office said last week that they’d learned about the explosion the same way Massner did: via the press release sent out by the Army on November 15.

Now, despite a court order blocking the detonation, the Army announced late Sunday night that it plans to blow up the lead azide on Wednesday, a day before the Thanksgiving holiday. (On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he was ordering the Army not to detonate anything without court approval.) Many Iowans are left with more questions than answers. Iowa’s unofficial state subreddit is filled with posts from people trying to plan holiday travel and safety around the event, which has switched dates twice in the past week. One local official in the path of a potential fallout told WIRED on Friday that she was leaving the area and staying at a hotel with her immunocompromised child.

Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the University of Iowa who has studied exposure to lead in his laboratory, says his lab has been “deluged with concerns,” with everyone from pediatricians to parents to people who run cleaning facilities and are worried about their staff exposure reaching out. Like most Iowans, Thorne also heard about the explosion from the Army’s press release.

“My first reaction was, They’re going to do what?” he says.

The 68 barrels of degraded lead azide at the Middletown site have been there for more than 20 years. In March, according to a document released by the Army on November 18, the material was officially labeled hazardous waste, and officials began looking into how to dispose of it. In a court filing published Saturday, the Army says that there is an “immediate risk” of the material exploding by itself after temperatures drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit. It is now invoking emergency powers to detonate the barrels by November 24.

“In short, a controlled detonation is by far safer than an uncontrolled explosion,” the filing states.

The Army did not immediately respond to a list of questions sent by WIRED.

The Army does seem to have looked into other options besides blowing up the azide. The New York Times reported Friday that the Army awarded a contract in late March to a private company to handle cleaning up the chemicals onsite. However, that contract was pulled two months later; the company told the Times that the Army did not give a reason for changing its mind on the cleanup. A contracting officer in the Army told the company that the Army’s decision to pursue detonation “was not based on deficiencies” with the company’s science.

In a letter sent to Governor Reynolds on Friday, the EPA Region 7 administrator said that the agency only learned that the material had degraded to a dangerous state in March. The letter also listed a number of strategies the EPA had considered besides detonation, including chemical cleanup, which also risked causing an explosion.

The Army has blown up expired munitions before, although not at the scale of what it plans to do in Iowa. Thorne says that any exposure to lead from the explosion is expected to be “quite a bit lower” than lead exposures in communities exposed to legacy pollution sources. But “there is no safe level for lead, especially for young children,” he says.

The Army did have some public meetings and communications in late October with officials in Middletown, where the explosion will take place and where it has recommended temporary evacuation measures for some neighborhoods. But it’s not clear why its initial direct outreach around public health didn’t extend to towns in potential fallout ranges for a blast, including Mediapolis, beyond asking for permission to test soil samples. (The Army did include recommended public health measures in its November 15 press release.)

Thorne, a former chair of the EPA’s Science Advisory Board, says that a successful public health outreach program has lots of opportunity for public engagement for all affected areas.

“You have public meetings. You answer questions. You have extensive Q&A and FAQs, and you have people speaking to why this is the only choice, what are the burdens, and some kind of a cost-benefit comparison between the options, and then you roll it out through the media, through social media, through many ways,” he says. “Best practice is not what they’ve done—I think this is closer to worst practice, from a public health perspective.”

For his part, Massner, Mediapolis’s mayor, said on Friday that he planned to take “standard precautions” and follow the Army’s public health recommendations. (The Army has not released fallout modeling for a Wednesday explosion, but if winds carry the material south, it would be possible for Mediapolis to no longer be in the affected zone.) But Massner says he understands why people in his town were freaked out.

“What people saw was the map they drew, which showed a [red] cloud going over everybody’s head. I don’t think that was the intent of the map,” he laughs. “When you see a map covered in red, you’re supposed to run for shelter immediately—your life is in danger.”

Update: 11/23/2026, 2:01 PM EDT: WIRED has updated the piece to clarify that President Donald Trump said he will defer to an appeals court on whether the material will be detonated.

entries.title: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is Nvidia’s Stock
entries.summary: Jensen Huang comes back, numbers go up. Maybe the reason behind the CEO’s return is just that simple?
entries.content:
Jensen Huang is back, baby, and Wall Street is thrilled.

The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO, and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the past month.

Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia’s board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”

And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back—with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.

Many questions remain unanswered. What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect?

The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies. Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles—the index’s biggest decline since March 2020.

On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded.

Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amid the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it, actually. The stock is up.”

According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!

entries.title: Jensen Huang Is Back as Nvidia CEO
entries.summary: The company’s board of directors has reinstated Huang a little more than a week after the CEO resigned amid allegations of multiple affairs, including with a direct report.
entries.content:
Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.

The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.

In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”

“I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.

In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.

Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.

President Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.”

Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with an Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.

Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.

Alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm, and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.

Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the company was primarily known within the gaming community. It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphics processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.

Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.

entries.title: Nvidia Is Powering Brain-Computer Interfaces Now
entries.summary: Brain-computer interface company Paradromics is using Nvidia’s computing hardware and software to process brain data.
entries.content:
A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.

Made by brain-computer interface company Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.

Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.

That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.

“We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle says. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.

“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.

Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.

Paradromics plans to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.

“Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.

Reducing lag time is important for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that users can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.

Through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, says AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means users won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.

Niewolny says he sees “tremendous potential for AI to expand human capability.” Nvidia is working with other players in the brain-computer interface space, including Synchron. The chipmaker will not have access to brain data through these partnerships, he says.

entries.title: 44 Best Gifts Under $100 That WIRED Loves (2026)
entries.summary: Score a great gift for everyone on your list without breaking the bank. Every one of these gifts comes WIRED-recommended.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

$100 is a sweet spot in gift-giving. You can really buy something that will make your giftee smile for that price without breaking the bank too much. To help, we spent countless hours testing all manner of gizmos and gadgets to bring you expert advice on what is worth buying.

If you don't mind spending more, check out our Best Tech Gifts guide, and if money is tight, we've also made a list of the Best Gifts Under $25. For giftees with a particular passion, you can find tailored options, like gifts for bird lovers, home chefs, book lovers, and more.

Updated November 2026: I added a few new entries and updated links and prices.

  • Portable Sound

    JBL

    Go 5

    The perfect tiny speaker, the JBL Go 5 fits in the palm of your hand but produces a surprisingly punchy sound with deep bass and clear mids. It's also tough, with an IP68 rating, offers plenty of connectivity options, and boasts battery life of up to 50 hours. It even supports stereo pairing if you have more than one.

    This is the budget pick in our Best Bluetooth Speakers guide.

  • Light It Up

    Govee

    Neon Rope Light Strip 2

    Most light strips are designed to be tucked away in recesses, but this Govee strip has a diffuser, so you can happily stick it anywhere you want without it being an eyesore. The adhesive-backed metal brackets make for easy installation too. The Govee app allows you to schedule, cycle through colors, play animations, and even create your own scenes. Some transitions are blocky, and the app can be confusing, but this is a great way to introduce your recipient to smart lights.

    This is our favorite diffused light strip from our Best Smart Lighting guide.

  • Tiny Tunes

    Stylophone

    Mini Playable Pocket Synthesizer Keychain

    Stupidly cute, this mini Stylophone on a keyring is a fully functional electronic synthesizer with a pop-out stylus, so you can noodle around with tunes wherever you are. Based on the original 1968 design, it comes in white, black, or pink, and the necessary AA batteries are included.

  • Power Up

    Nimble

    Champ Portable Charger

    Sling a good portable charger in your bag, and you will never be stranded with a dead phone again. One of our favorites is Nimble's Champ, which is compact, light, and packs a 5,000- to 20,000-mAh capacity, capable of recharging most phones and laptops at least once, fully at its smallest size. It comes in snazzy speckled colors with a handy lanyard strap and a small USB-C cable. We are also big fans of Nimble’s environmental efforts (using bioplastics and plastic-free packaging).

    This power bank appears in our Best Portable Chargers guide.

  • A Smart Speaker

    Google

    Home Speaker

    The Google Home Speaker is our favorite smart speaker right now. It boasts impressive sound for its small form, the AI is a little more human than competitors, and it comes in a range of fun colors. Gemini is also helpful and smart, though some of the best features require a subscription.

    This speaker is the top pick in our Best Smart Speakers guide.

  • Cyberpunk Original

    Ace Books

    Neuromancer: Deluxe Edition

    It’s hard to believe Neuromancer was released in 1984. William Gibson’s sci-fi novel was foundational to the cyberpunk scene, and the hit 2020 video game Cyberpunk 2077 borrows heavily from it. Ahead of Apple TV’s new show, which arrives in January 2027, Penguin’s Ace Books has released this special edition with fresh cover art and sprayed edges. It can be a challenging read, but it’s an incredibly inventive and spookily prescient masterpiece.

  • Desk Tidy

    Oakywood

    Headphone Stand with Wireless Charger

    We love multifunctional gadgets like this headphone stand from Oakywood, which offers a place to hang your cans and a spot to wirelessly charge your phone. The angular base in solid walnut or oak is super stylish, and the steel stand keeps your headphones neatly out of the way.

    This headphone stand appears in our Best Wireless Chargers guide.

  • Game On

    Comfy to hold for long gaming sessions, with a subtle texture that adds grip, this mobile controller combines responsive analog sticks with clicky buttons and an excellent D-pad. It cradles your phone with a built-in USB-C connector for a speedy connection and includes pass-through charging, a screenshot or screen-recording button, a mute button, and a headphone jack. There's also a handy companion app with an optional subscription.

    This is a top pick in our Best Mobile Controllers guide.

  • Motion Sensor

    Kinisium

    Kini SafeAlert Wi-Fi Motion Sensor

    This versatile motion sensor can flag access to a cabinet, drawer, or safe. You can easily configure it in the app to set exactly what triggers an alert, set the cooldown period, and choose how you want to receive alerts. Unlike many other smart home devices, it keeps everything completely private too.

    This gadget appears in our Best Motion Sensors guide.

  • Forty Winks

    LectroFan

    Evo Sound Machine

    I have a constant whining tinnitus sound in my ears after a misspent youth of loud gigs and clubs. A white-noise machine helps me tune it out at night so I can drift off to sleep. This is what I have on my nightstand right now, and it works great. Compact, easy to use, and with 22 non-repeating sounds (I like the ocean surf) and a timer function, it's all you need.

    This gadget appears in our Best Sound Machines guide.

  • Wireless Keyboard

    Keychron

    B2 Pro

    One of the best scissor-switch keyboards available, the Keychron B2 Pro offers a comfortable, quiet typing experience. Its fully customizable (you can use Keychron’s Launcher software to remap keys and set up macros), and it looks pretty stylish, too.

    You’ll also find this deck in our Best Keyboards guide.

  • Gaming Mouse

    SteelSeries

    Rival 3 Gen 2

    You don’t have to spend big to snag a great gaming mouse, and the SteelSeries Rival 3 proves it. This mouse is lightweight and responsive, with a lovely rubbery scroll wheel and a couple of handy side buttons. It’s everything most people need without the unnecessary frills.

    This is the budget pick in our Best Gaming Mice guide.

  • Excellent Earbuds

    JLab Audio

    Go Pop ANC

    These full-featured earbuds have it all. Solid sound, active noise cancellation that works well, a stable Bluetooth connectivity, and a robust app with adjustable EQ and programmable controls. It even has a respectable IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating.

    These are the cheapest option in our Best Wireless Earbuds guide.

  • Cordless Vac

    Hoto

    Penvac Cordless Handheld Vacuum Cleaner

    Crumbs in your keyboard, dirt in your window frames, those dusty crevices in your car: Our lives are filled with mucky, but hard-to-clean places. My own personal vacuum has a bag of attachments, but it’s heavy and a hassle to pull out and set up. Hoto’s angled Penvac is the cordless solution. The battery doesn’t last long, suction drops as it fills, and it’s a pain to empty, but my nooks and crannies have never been so dust-free.

entries.title: Submit Your Questions: Will Anyone Keep You Safe From AI?
entries.summary: Experts agree that AI, in one way or another, poses real danger. Will the industry do anything about it? Join our livestream on December 2 to hear your questions answered.
entries.content:
The AI safety conversation, as Lauren Goode put it, has lost the plot. Will the technology really kill us all? Should each one of us be worried about cyberattacks by rogue agents? Will it bring on total societal collapse? Though there’s room for disagreement about which catastrophe is most salient, experts are aligned on the idea that society is, for one reason or another, in real trouble. This begs one big question: What are industry leaders doing to mitigate the danger they’ve unleashed? Though a pause in training models, a data center moratorium, and other regulation has been proposed, the industry hasn’t exactly made changes that are putting people at ease around AI safety. Meanwhile, critical infrastructure seems more and more vulnerable every day. We’re gathering our Backchannel team, who will deploy their expertise on the ins and outs of Big Tech and AI safety, to answer all your questions.

Bring all your questions about Big Tech and AI safety to WIRED’s next, subscriber-only livestream scheduled for December 2 at noon ET / 9am PT. To leave questions in advance, head to the comment section below.

The event will be streamed right here. For subscribers who are not able to join, a replay of the livestream will be available after the event. Not a subscriber yet? Subscribe now to get access to this livestream, plus full access to WIRED.

On the Panel:

  • Sandra Upson: a features editor at WIRED, and the editor of the Backchannel newsletter.
  • Steven Levy: WIRED’s editor at large, who’s been contributing to the magazine since its inception and covering technology for over three decades. He cowrites Backchannel.
  • Lauren Goode: a senior correspondent at WIRED, covering all things Silicon Valley and cowriting Backchannel.

For more stories on AI safety, check out our ongoing series where we assess the real threats of AI.

In the meantime, check out past livestreams on women in tech, the defense tech industry, and the future of electric vehicles.

entries.title: Best Gifts for Parents (and Their Babies): Bottle Washers, Prepared Meals, and More
entries.summary: If your friend is in the depths of newborn survival, these gifts and gadgets can go a long way to help make parenting a little easier.
entries.content:
Parenting is exhausting. If there’s a new parent in your life, whether it’s your friend who is the new parent of the group or a family member who just had a baby, there are a lot of ways to show some love. Showing up, checking in on how they're surviving, and bringing something that can improve their life are all great ways to support the new parents in your circle.

There’s a lot of parenting and baby gear out there, and not all of it is created equal. Not all of it will suit what the parents in your life might need, either. This guide is organized into a handful of categories of parenting gadgets, smart home gear, little luxuries, and even food deliveries you can send to their door. All of these are tried and tested by WIRED’s reviewers, many of whom are parents and can confirm the difference it’s made in their lives.

Looking for more baby gear or gift ideas? Don’t miss our gifts for moms and dads or our guide to all the best baby gear.

Updated November 2026: We've added the Calpak Car Organizer, Solly Baby Wrap, and Tubby Todd's gift sets as new gifts to this guide, and a discount code for CookUnity.

Featured Gifts

Great Parenting Gadgets to Gift

It’s easy to remember to register for things like the car seat and baby clothes. But there are a lot of small gadgets that make parenting a little easier, things that new parents don’t realize they might love using. Here are some of the favorites from the parents at WIRED.

Something to Eat

Early parenting is survival, and bandwidth to go to the grocery store or cook becomes a hard zero. There’s a reason friends and family often run food trains for new parents. The following food gifts would be a great option to contribute to a food train, and being shippable packages means you can send them to a friend or family member you may live too far from to visit often.

Some Daily Life Upgrades

I didn’t put anything fun on my firstborn's registry. I was so overwhelmed with how many must-haves I needed (including an infant baby tub device I never used, but every registry site claimed I'd need). Baby registry websites will constantly tell you that you haven’t added things from every single category their site has deemed important. There are a lot of things parents need, but there are lots of fun things you can gift that aren’t necessities but will still make parenting a little easier, or at least feel like a thoughtful gift.

Smart Home Improvements

I’m biased as a smart home reviewer, but the right Wi-Fi–powered gadget could change your life, especially when you’re locked into a contact nap and need to dim the lights without moving. These are a few smart home upgrades I’d recommend gifting to just about anyone, new parent or not.

Gifts for Little One

You probably already gifted the baby something at the baby shower, but if you want to get something for the little one to play with, here are some of our favorite baby toys as WIRED parents.

Smart Splurge Gifts

If you’re looking to spend a little more on the new parents, these smart home and connected gadgets will genuinely improve their everyday life. When I tell you that every parent I’ve hooked on a good robot vacuum comes back to me raving about how much it’s helped them—it’s worth the price of entry. If you’re looking for true parenting gear, like the best baby monitors and smart bassinets, I’d check out my guide to the Best Baby Gear instead.

entries.title: A Former DOGE Operative Won a Federal Contract. Then Things Got Messy
entries.summary: Canadian citizen Yat Choi moved from DOGE to the National Design Studio before launching his own company, Govmaxxing.
entries.content:
Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a company owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

At the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

The bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”

In October, a company called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his company made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

Perez says that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his company’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

“I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” says Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”

According to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

“HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” says HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former government employee who wants to talk about what's happening? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporters securely on Signal at velliott88.18.

Choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and said in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Big Balls” Coristine.

In December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi announced in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his company, GovMaxxing, through which he plans to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

In response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi says that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

Choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

On his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s company was not registered in the state of New York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” says Choi.

Choi says that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”

According to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, says that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”

Choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was announced. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or company, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman says that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

On the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the company as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

But Tillipman says that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”

Choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez launched an AI defense technology company called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

Despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a company to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”
